author: David Hytner at the Riyadh Air Metropolitano
description:
• England top Nations League group after 3-2 win with 10 men

  • Tuchel: ‘What a performance we put out there’

Thomas Tuchel hailed England’s 3-2 Nations League win over Spain at the Eastadio Metropolitano as a statement result and the best performance of his tenure. The manager watched his team surge into a 3-0 lead before the tone of a pulsating night changed when Elliot Anderson was sent off in the 63rd minute in the act of conceding a penalty.

Mikel Oyarzabal scored from the spot and when Nico Williams pulled another goal back, England were forced to hang on. They got a memorable victory over the line thanks to a series of stunning James Trafford saves; the best was the double stop in added time to deny Fermín López and then Aymeric Laporte.
title: Tuchel hails England’s statement win over Spain as ‘complete performance’

author: Hannah Al-Othman
description:
Calls for government to issue formal apology to those investigated after ending pregnancies in England and Wales

Campaigners and women previously convicted of illegal abortions have hailed a “historic day” after the pardoning of every woman who has faced criminal investigation for ending a pregnancy during the last 150 years.

A vote in the House of Lords earlier this year introduced legislation to pardon women accused of terminating their own pregnancies outside the legal framework and expunge their criminal records, under section 242 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026, which takes effect on Monday.

Continue reading...
title: Women prosecuted for abortions hail ‘historic day’ after receiving pardon

author: Harry Taylor
description:
Duke of Sussex meets wounded veterans in city and says country could one day host Invictus Games

Prince Harry has told Ukrainian soldiers they are going to win the war with Russia, during a surprise visit to the country.

The Duke of Sussex met wounded veterans and medics in the city of Lviv, in the west of Ukraine, as he addressed a conference on treating those injured in war. He said he had taken a risk in travelling to the country, but that he had felt “warmth” when arriving on Saturday.

Continue reading...
title: Prince Harry tells Ukrainians they are ‘going to win war’ on surprise trip to Lviv

author: David Hytner at the Estadio Metropolitano
description:
It was the game to show Thomas Tuchel where his rebooted England team had got to; surely the ultimate test in international football. Spain in Spain. A world champion team who, in Tuchel’s words, had “forgotten how to lose.” Before this Nations League tie, they had been beaten only once in 43 matches – on penalties to Portugal in the final of this competition last year.

What England produced for 65 minutes here in Madrid was extraordinary. What followed was equally so for very different reasons. And when it was all over, England had the most sensational of victories.

Continue reading...
title: England fend off fiery Spain fightback after Anderson’s red to top Nations League group

author: Beau Dure
description:
• Players meet for end of year championship

  • Sabalenka apologizes to Svitolina after outburst

Also today is the WTA Finals doubles … well, final. What do you call the final of the Finals? Metafinals? Superfinals?

US player Taylor Townsend and Czechia’s Katerina Siniakova will face the Italian duo of Sara Errani and Jasmine Paolini. That’s coming up after the singles final, which is imminent.

Continue reading...
title: WTA Finals final: Elina Svitolina v Mirra Andreeva – live

author: Alexandra Topping, Political correspondent
description:
Professor calls on ministers to use awareness triggered by Russell Brand conviction to examine use of rape myths in trials

The debate triggered by high profile cases must “pull back the curtain” on the treatment of people making allegations of sexual offences in the criminal justice system in England and Wales, the government’s independent adviser on rape has told the Guardian.

Prof Katrin Hohl, who has advised the government in an overhaul of how rape is treated by police forces and the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), said the government should use the public awareness triggered by Russell Brand’s conviction for rape to examine the use of rape myths and jury direction in trials.
title: ‘Pull back the curtain’ on treatment of sexual assault victims in court, says UK government adviser

author: Associated Press
description:
Oklahoma man, 73, executed for killing ex’s estranged husband, as US nears 40 executions for second straight year

A Texas man convicted of fatally stabbing and beheading his three young children in a squalid, windowless apartment in 2003 was recently executed.

John Allen Rubio, 46, was pronounced dead at 6.47 pm on Thursday after a lethal injection at the state prison in Huntsville, Texas. His killings of his baby girl and two toddlers so rocked the city of Brownsville on the US border with Mexico that the apartment building was later demolished – and the land turned into a park and community garden.

Continue reading...
title: Texas puts to death man who beheaded three children, hours after Oklahoma execution

author: Agencies
description:
• Brazil legend plays first half for Serie C club at age 46

  • ‘Is this my last one? I don’t know,’ Ronaldinho says

Ronaldinho played 45 minutes on his return to professional football in Italy. The 46-year-old Brazil great announced in June that he had signed for the Serie C side Ravenna, 11 years after he appeared to have brought his illustrious career to a close with Fluminense.

Five months later, he was in the starting lineup as Ravenna faced their local rivals Forlì. Ronaldinho, wearing the No 10 shirt, entered the stadium to great fanfare, with the 5,000-capacity Stadio Bruno Benelli adding a temporary 1,800-capacity stand – dubbed “R10” – for the occasion. Flares and smoke bombs were let off in the stands while Andrea Bocelli’s Con Te Partiro blasted out of the stadium’s speakers.

Continue reading...</
title: Ronaldinho makes debut for Italian side Ravenna after 11-year hiatus in playing career

author: Daniel Harris
description:
• Updates from 7.45pm (GMT) kick-off in Madrid

  • Get in touch: email Daniel and follow us on BlueSky

The scandal of England’s World Cup semi-final capitulation is already enshrined in the extensive annals of mythological failure; failure so gloriously tepid and inept it’s barely failure at all, rather a perfectly pitched lyrical paean to the sacred, desperate art of getting in your own way as wimpishly as possible. It is beautiful.

The truth, though – and part of the beauty – is it remains an ultimately futile act. Let’s say England see out the win, setting up a final meeting with Spain: Emlyn, what happened next?

Continue reading...
title: Spain v England: Nations League – live

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Paul English says the cheap home charging that makes EVs economical is out of reach for many, while Mike Hawes wonders if consumers are ready to switch. Plus letters from Ben Plowden and Anne Maclennan

George Monbiot is right that European carmakers have dragged their feet, but his column describes only half the problem (Why are Britain’s streets still so polluted? Because the car industry dinosaurs do what they like, and politicians let them, 11 November). About 40% of UK households have no off-street parking, rising to around 60% in urban areas.

For us, the cheap home charging that makes electric vehicles (EVs) economical is out of re
title: Electric vehicle targets and reality are now on a collision course | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Readers respond to an editorial which argues that the agency’s maps are still a superior way to navigate the landscape

I loved your homage to the original mapmakers of the Ordnance Survey, giving credit to those who hauled their theodolites around the country to take their measurements (Editorial, 8 November).

Credit also should be given to the mathematicians, and especially the computers (people who did the arithmetic for hour after hour) who took the field measurements and converted them to coordinates to plot on a paper map.

Continue reading...
title: Ordnance Survey maps go the extra mile  | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Jo Barlow kept chickens for more than 15 years and found them to be intelligent, brave and funny

Whoever deemed chickens synonymous with cowardice obviously didn’t tell my 14-year‑old bantam who took on a hungry Harris hawk and won (Chickens are synonymous with cowardice. Is it time to stick up for our feathered friends?, 11 November).

I kept chickens for more than 15 years and found them to be intelligent, unique characters who could be brave, funny, naughty, loving and kind in equal measure.

Continue reading...
title: Chickens are great characters, not cowards | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Prof Ian Convery and Rebecca Wrigley respond to concerns that the eagles would destroy seabird populations

Your article (Reintroduction of white-tailed eagles puts seabird colonies at risk of wipeout, say experts, 8 November) raises important questions, but overlooks a fundamental point: eagles and seabirds coexisted around Britain’s coastline for thousands of years before eagles were driven to extinction through human persecution. Predation and disturbance are therefore not novel ecological pressures, but historically established interactions that have been absent from much of the British landscape for over a century.

There is a danger here of accepting an ecologically impoverished landscape as our conservation baseline. Seabird colonies have existed in the absence of a native apex predator, but that
title: The ecological value of reintroducing white-tailed eagles to Britain | Letters

author: Gerard Meagher
description:
• Chessum, Atkinson and full-back Furbank back from injury

  • England expect backlash after New Zealand defeat in Wales

England have welcomed back the cavalry for the crunch clash against the All Blacks on Saturday with George Furbank, Ollie Chessum and Seb Atkinson all returning to the squad from injury.

Steve Borthwick’s side are braced for a backlash after New Zealand’s first defeat against Wales in 73 years but the head coach is boosted with three key men on course to make their comebacks this weekend.

Continue reading...
title: England handed boost for All Blacks clash with Furbank leading return of cavalry

author: Editorial
description:
Renewed commitments to electrification and climate science are vital outcomes from the latest round of UN talks

The Cop31 climate talks have acquired something their delegates scarcely expected: a little political breathing space. The comeback by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the second round of Brazil’s presidential race was important for many reasons. Victory for his opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, would have marked a dangerous retreat from democracy. But Mr Bolsonaro’s commitment to environmental deregulation would also have spelled disaster for the Amazon, making Lula’s re-election a big win for the climate. Similarly, success by Democrats in the
title: The Guardian view on Cop31: the green transition must not be derailed | Editorial

author: Editorial
description:
Whitehall needs to change, but more technology isn’t enough. Opening routes to leadership would bring skills that are too often overlooked

The cabinet secretary, Antonia Romeo, called for an overhaul of a “reactive and risk-averse” civil service in her speech last Tuesday. Ministers planned a “radical shift” of powers, resources and accountability to regional and local government, which she said would leave Whitehall “leaner and more strategic”. As 80% of civil servants already work outside London, devolution promises to alter what central government does, not simply where it operates. Reinvention is in the civil service’s blood – ever since it was founded as a permanent, impartial institution in 1854. Even departmental boundaries, Dame Antonia said, are on notice,
title: The Guardian view on civil service reform: AI cannot conjure a capable state on its own | Editorial

author: Andy Burnham
description:
Alan Milburn’s review will mark a watershed moment for our approach to welfare and childhood. This is how I’m determined to create change

  • Report: Burnham pledges early intervention and ‘benefits backstop’ to tackle youth jobs crisis

A generation of young people did not wake up one morning and decide they did not want to work. The fact that a million 16- to 24-year-olds are now not in education, employment or training (Neet) is not their fault. It is ours, as politicians.

We have failed to give them the support they need as they have grown up in a tougher world. This has become an economic catastrophe for the country – and a moral one too.

Andy
title: The crisis facing Britain’s young people is politicians’ fault. To fix it, we need a generational response | Andy Burnham

author: Michael Sainato
description:
Two people injured after wingtip of Copa Airlines Boeing 737 struck nose of United Parcel Service Boeing 767

Two planes collided with one another on a taxiway at Miami’s international airport on Saturday night – a day after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued an hours-long nationwide ground stop due to communication issues affecting multiple air traffic control centers.

In a statement, the Trump administration-led FAA said the wingtip of a Copa Airlines Boeing 737 struck the nose of a United Parcel Service Boeing 767 “while the airplanes were taxiing at Miami International Airport”.

Continue reading...
title: Two planes collide on taxiway at Miami airport one day after national grounding

author: Brian Coney
description:
Ulster Hall, Belfast
With two sets of fathers and sons now in the group, as they play all of Moseley Shoals on its 30th anniversary, the indie stalwarts have aged into seismic and soulful performers

‘It’s only 30 years ago,” Simon Fowler says of Moseley Shoals. He would seem to mean it, but 30 years makes Ocean Colour Scene’s breakthrough album as old now as Revolver was when they were making it. The band once derided for raiding the 60s are now heritage themselves. They open the album’s anniversary tour on the stage where Led Zeppelin first played Stairway to Heaven, and you can’t help but appreciate the lineage.

They walk on to Green Onions, fresh from the Crown Bar, and open with You’ve Got It Bad, all supreme Motown stomp. Fowler sings with a hand in his pocket and looks taken aback by the welcome. The casualness is a conduit: his voice has aged
title: Ocean Colour Scene review – no other band of their era can do it like this

author: Erica Jeal
description:
Glyndebourne, Lewes
Lucy Armstrong’s family opera transports audiences to a secret world above the rooftops. It explores themes of grief and loss with a lightness of touch, and is directed, designed and performed with panache.

For decades now, Glyndebourne has been setting the bar for what a youth opera company can be. Its latest show is Spark, a new full-length opera directed by Fiona Dunn with music by Lucy Armstrong, exploring grownup themes of grief and loss.

Spark is a story of a parallel world accessed via something unlikely, so there are shades of Narnia or Wonderland. Our heroine is Clara (shades of The Nutcracker), who has panic attacks when she tries to go to school: “They talk like it’s simple,” she says in Olivia Bell’s succinct, fluent libretto, “but my chest is tightening and I can’t breathe.” We find out that her anxiety stems from her grief for her brother, and that she can no longer connect with her parents, who are hav
title: Spark review – Glyndebourne Youth Opera light up a terrific new show of monsters and magic

author: Zach Vasquez
description:
The comic returns for the seventh time for the best episode so far this season which takes aim at tech bros and brings back a former cast member as guest

This edition of Saturday Night Live opens at the CIA headquarters. In the wake of the Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stepping down after details of his extramarital affairs, including one with an accused Chinese spy, came to light, the agency has called together a meeting of the nation’s top tech billionaires: creepy Peter Thiel (James Austin Johnson), robotic Sam Altman (Ben Marshall), awkward Dario Amodei (Jane Wickline), and the insufferable duo of Mark Zuckerberg (Andy Dismukes) and Elon Musk (Jeremy Culhane).

An agent (tonight’s host, John Mulaney) attempts to school them on how not to get honeypotted. Per a helpful Venn diagram: “On this side we have beautiful women, and on this side we have people who would be interested in your shared opinions and interests. I cannot stress this enough: there is no overlap.” He fails
title: Saturday Night Live: is John Mulaney the best modern host we have?

author: Mark Brown North of England correspondent
description:
Four arrested after BMW collides with Volkswagen on Gelderd Road, with police appealing for witnesses

Two people aged 22 and 23 have died after their car was hit by a BMW being pursued by police.

West Yorkshire police said four people had been arrested after the crash in Leeds on Sunday and appealed for witnesses to come forward.

Continue reading...
title: Two killed in Leeds after car pursued by police crashes into another vehicle

description:
The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on subjects ranging from trivial flights of fancy to profound scientific and philosophical concepts

  • Readers reply: Why is sugar-free tonic water always described as ‘slimline’?

I recently made a return trip to Edinburgh from London on which both legs of the journey were either significantly delayed or cancelled. At Waverley station, a message over the public address system told us we could travel by any “reasonable” route, but what does that mean? What counts as reasonable and what doesn’t? And who decides? Grant, by email

Post your answers (and new questions) below or send them to nq@theguardian.com. A selection will be published next Sunday.
title: When does a reasonable train route become unreasonable?

author: Robert Booth UK technology editor
description:
Exclusive: South Wales police figures show BAME people accounted for 24% of selected scans in 2025, despite being 7% of population

Ethnic minority people are four times more likely than their white counterparts to be chosen for some police facial scans, according to official data, sparking warnings of racial bias.

Internal figures released by South Wales police revealed that 24% of people selected by police for facial recognition checks were from ethnic minorities, despite this group making up only 7% of the area’s total population.

Continue reading...
title: Ethnic minority groups in Wales four times more likely to be target of police facial scans

author: Ali Stevens
description:
Ali Stevens’ daughter was a baby when they discovered she has a syndrome which causes deafblindness. There’s no roadmap for change – but what gets her through is the same as for any parent

My daughter Poppy is five. She’s energetic and curious, loves dresses, books and creating new things and spends a lot of time playing with her big sister, Evie.

When Poppy was born, my husband, Ben, and I were focused on the usual joys of welcoming a new baby. A routine hearing screening showed something wasn’t quite right, although initially we were told it was probably fluid in her ears.

Continue reading...
title: Our five-year-old has hearing loss and may one day be blind. Here is where I find hope

author: Dave Schilling
description:
After a hack in France, internet-enabled appliances are looking even less appealing – especially before the holidays

We are deep into the holiday season now, past Halloween and a mere two weeks away from American Thanksgiving.

I’ve already given up taking care of my body, surrendering fully to gluttony, vices, and going to bed at 7pm because it’s pitch black outside. I’ve begun to hibernate like a slothful bear, my blanket and pillow never too far from my grasp. The only thing closer to my hands than my bedsheets is a slice of cold pizza. I just want to eat in peace, thank you very much.

Continue reading...
title: Why would anyone want a smart fridge?  | Dave Schilling

author: Tim Dowling
description:
About 1.6 million people in the UK have this agonising condition, but it is often viewed as a comical malady brought on by overconsumption and idleness. What can be done to end the stigma?

Brett McAllister-Byrne was in his early 30s when he first noticed a sharp ache in his ankle and big toe. “I felt it the night after playing football, and I thought I must have had a knock or something,” he says. “But then it just got worse and worse.” The next morning McAllister-Byrne, an urban planner, was in too much pain to go to work. When he described the episode to his family, they suggested it might be gout.

“I was like, really?” he says. “Can you get that in your 30s?”

Continue reading...
title: Gout is on the rise – and excruciating. Why are sufferers still judged for it?

author: Emma Beddington
description:
People in my age group are experiencing poorer physical and mental health than their elders at the same stage. Is this down to UPFs and booze, or something more complicated?

I almost choked on my bird-food breakfast recently, reading that gen Xers are in worse health than boomers. Research by the UCL Centre for Longitudinal Studies, on approximately 8,000 participants aged about 50 from the 1970 British Cohort Study, found that my generation is experiencing “worse physical and mental health across adulthood than earlier-born generations”.

Come on! How? We have better health education and pharmaceuticals than any previous generation, we’ve been browbeaten into cultivating our microbiomes and hitting our step counts, harassed to stand up (sitting’s worse than smoking!), jump around (protect your bones!) and pop creatine (uns
title: Gen X is in worse health than boomers – and I have a few theories as to why | Emma Beddington

author: Jackson Ryan
description:
Headlines have claimed the release of the first new GTA game in 13 years will hugely affect the global economy on Thursday – but there’s another story that’s been left behind

A new pandemic is threatening planet Earth. It’s scheduled to hit 19 November. Entire offices and worksites will be emptied; employees struck down by a mysterious illness. But you need not panic: it isn’t fatal. It should pass in a few days.

The anticipation for Grand Theft Auto VI, the first new game in the franchise in 13 years, is so high that a steady stream of news coverage has suggested it heralds economic catastrophe due to workers taking time off to play the game. The term “GTA Flu” was coined for the swathe of sickies that reportedly happened when GTA V was released in 2013, and – supposedly – are set to happen again when GTA VI comes out this week.

Continue reading...
title: ‘Grand Theft Auto Flu’: is the whole world really taking the day off work to play GTA VI?

author: Felicity Cloake
description:
Slow-cooked pork in a deliciously sweet-salty glaze is Vietnamese comfort food at its best

Many moons ago, I attended a cookery class in Hanoi that revealed to me the glories of thịt kho tàu, a simple but unbelievably delicious dish of caramelised pork braised in sweet coconut water and savoury fish sauce, enlivened by plenty of black pepper. In fact, loved it so much that I put their version in my cookbook, The A to Z of Eating, and then somehow forgot all about it for a decade. It’s easy to do that when you’re always working on the next recipe, but this week has been a very welcome rediscovery, not least because I’ve learned a lot more about what chef Thuy Diem Pham describes in her book The Little Viet Kitchen as “the ultimate home comfort food”.

A family favourite, it’s also traditionally serve
title: How to make the perfect Vietnamese caramel pork, or thit kho – recipe | Felicity Cloake's How to make the perfect …

author: Peter Stonein Washington
description:
Courts have issued stinging rebukes to president’s ‘blatant’ financial ploys as pro-democracy groups defend ‘government of laws, not of men’ pillar

Donald Trump’s legal and political ploys to increase his wealth and boost Republican electoral prospects have fueled lawsuits by non-partisan groups, prompting federal judges to issue stinging rejections to some of the president’s schemes.

Several lawsuits were filed in 2026 against Trump’s schemes to benefit his bottom line by reducing potential tax liabilities, boosting his Truth Social platform financially by offering big investors early access to his posts, and helping Republicans by using federal funds to pay for highly partisan ads touting Trump’s record in the run-up to the midterm elections, in which Republicans suffered a heavy defeat.

Continue reading...
title: ‘Shameless venality’: how a flurry of lawsuits has thwarted Trump’s self-enrichment schemes

author: Zoe Wood
description:
From Aldi candles to Quince’s cashmere jumpers, cut-price versions of high-end sellers have gone mainstream. But is it fair?

For fans of the festive season nothing is more Christmassy than lighting a super-sized botanical candle with its trim of orange slices and berries.

But as the notes of cinnamon and clove fill the room will you be burning money spent on the White Company’s £95 “winter indulgence” candle that customers describe as the “scent of Christmas”. Or have you followed TikTok’s advice and bought the Aldi “dupe” for £25.

Continue reading...
title: Christmas ‘dupes’: the cheaper gift versions proving a festive hit in the cost of living crisis

author: Gautam Malkani
description:
The UN’s annual climate conference began in Turkey this week. Reporting from the event can be gruelling work – but it’s also crucial.

They are counting on you not to read our coverage of the Cop31 climate talks. Fossil fuel companies, climate science deniers, petrostates, far right populists … They want you to think the negotiations are too intractable, the progress too halting, the issues too complex, too tortuous, too pointless, TL;DR.

But as the UN’s 31st annual climate conference got underway in Antalya, Turkey this week, our journalists have been g
title: ‘It is not unusual to go 48 hours with little sleep’: what it’s like to cover a Cop climate summit

author: Peter Bevan
description:
Whether you want minimalist or heritage, waterproof or suede, our menswear expert has rounded up the most stylish pairs for every occasion and outfit

• The best men’s coats for autumn and winter

I haven’t always worn boots. For years I wrote them off – at 5ft 8in, I was convinced anything above the ankle would make my legs look shorter. Then I started wearing them with the right trousers – a straight leg that falls over the top – and realised I’d spent a decade getting winter wrong. All anyone sees is a smart pair of shoes that happens to keep your ankles warm.

Here’s the thing: boots needn’t be intimidating. They’re just the wintry version of the leather shoes you already own. A chelsea is your loafer – it goes with pretty much everything in your wardrobe and every event in your diary, Christmas parties included. A der
title: The 14 best men’s boots for winter, from chelseas and lace-ups to wellies

author: Alexandra Topping Political correspondent
description:
Author of major review into youth unemployment rejects ‘crude cuts’ to payments and downplays opposition to his proposals within Labour

Alan Milburn has said “there is no such thing as a free lunch”, in response to critics who believe the government should make tougher cuts to out-of-work benefits for young people.

The former health secretary will publish a major review on Tuesday, urging ministers to implement radical reforms to address the UK’s youth unemployment crisis, which has seen the number of young people not in employment, education or training (Neet) rise to about a million.

Continue reading...
title: ‘No such thing as a free lunch,’ says Milburn as he warns it will take a decade for UK benefits bill to come down

author: Arifa Akbar
description:
Orange Tree theatre, London
This streamlined adaptation of Elizabeth Gaskell’s novel gets right to the heart of her characters, who face heartbreak and loss but gain from the strength of female friendship

There’s more than one worry for any new dramatisation of Elizabeth Gaskell’s novel to contend with. There is the risk of this story, set among the unmarried women and widows of a fictional English town, being considered Middlemarch lite – and overshadowed by the Royal Shakespeare Company’s luminous adaptation of the George Eliot novel, currently running in Stratford-Upon-Avon. Then there is the 2007 BBC adaptation of Cranford, which threw every national treasure at it, trowelling on the loveable humour and sentiment as it did so.

This production, however, co-created by Lin Coghlan, Shaun McKenna an
title: Tamsin Greig is sensational in a Cranford where comedy and pain are in perfect balance

author: Press Association
description:
• Secures top-two finish at DP World Tour Championship

  • McIlroy finishes on -10 as Tyrell Hatton wins event

Rory McIlroy edged out Eugenio Chacarra to claim a record-equalling eighth Race to Dubai title with a second-place finish at the DP World Tour Championship, where Tyrrell Hatton sealed a five-shot victory.

Spaniard Chacarra had held a slender 533.93-point lead over Masters champion McIlroy going into the season finale at Jumeirah Golf Estates.

Continue reading...
title: Rory McIlroy wins golf’s Race to Dubai title for record-equalling eighth time

author: Richard Partington
description:
This week’s long-awaited review will call for benefit cuts but lack of entry-level jobs is also driving the crisis

  • ‘I’m scared about my future’: young people on the stress and desperation of jobseeking

A generation is being sold short. Almost a million young people are not in education, employment or training (Neet). Austerity and the Covid pandemic cast a lengthy shadow, AI is upending the jobs market, and the cost of living is soaring – all under the microscope of the social media age.

This week Alan Milburn’s landmark report on young people and work will bring Britain to a fork in the road: either continue on this path of state and market failure or sharply change direction.

Continue reading...
title: Bad jobs or benefits? Milburn should force employers to help the young | Richard Partington

author: John Harris
description:
Nearly 2 million children are housed in dire conditions, anxious families are living out of carrier bags. There’s little sign of the hope our PM promised

Two days after the Christmas of 2024, Andy Burnham put up a post on X that linked to a piece about housing in the Guardian. The then mayor of Greater Manchester, who was beginning to find his voice as a frank critic of Keir Starmer’s new government, did not mess about: “The Government should make building hundreds of thousands of council homes its defining purpose,” he said. “No other policy, achievable within a parliament, would have greater social and economic benefits.”

In his first Labour conference speech as party leader and prime minister, Burnham reprised much the same argument, promising “the biggest council housebuilding programme since the
title: Is Burnham’s plan for a housing revolution anything more than a pipedream? | John Harris

author: Eric Berger
description:
High-profile crimes and disease outbreaks obscure the fact that the big ships are largely safe – and seeing record numbers of bookings

This month, there has been a swell of stories about things going wrong on cruises.

A man was arrested in Texas after he allegedly killed a woman during a voyage through the Caribbean. A pianist on a Royal Caribbean cruise from California was rescued by two fishers in the Pacific Ocean after he went overboard. And Singapore seized the MV Odyssey, a US-operated cruise ship that was supposed to offer retirees a “permanent” life at sea. The operator ran out of money because of increased fuel prices and dropped all its passengers off in Cambodia.

Continue
title: ‘You unpack once’: despite reports of ‘poop cruises’ and murder, cruise ships are more popular than ever

author: Ali Martin at Adelaide Oval
description:
As much as the sandpaper soap opera continued to deal in alternative facts on Sunday, recollections of this second one-day international are unlikely to differ. For Tom Banton and Gus Atkinson, architects of an emphatic 135-run victory for England that levelled the series, it was unquestionably a match to remember.

Banton was sublime after England were asked to bat first, unfurling a crisp 121 from just 99 balls to underpin an imposing total of 355 for six. No touring side had ever gone bigger on Australian soil – the ideal platform for Harry Brook’s pace attack to release the handbrake and level this three-match series.

Continue reading...
title: Banton’s century leads England to emphatic win in second ODI amid Australian soap opera

author: Kim Willsher in Paris
description:
New exhibition restores painter’s place as leading figure in French movement that revolutionised art

As a painter, friend, and collaborator of Edgar Degas, who exhibited with impressionist artists including Claude Monet and Camille Pissarro, Mary Cassatt was at the heart of the 19th-century movement that emerged in France and revolutionised art.

She was also a woman and foreign – “American, American through and through” is how she described herself. As a result, in the 100 years since her death, Cassatt has been frequently overlooked in the country where she produced her best work.

Continue reading...
title: Reclaiming Mary Cassatt: putting overlooked American artist back at heart of impressionism

author: Michael Aylwin
description:
Seismic victory in Cardiff was cathartic and though Steve Tandy urges caution, maybe the ‘Welsh problem’ can be fixed

So that’s that fixed then. Wales are back, and all is right with the world. Suddenly the dysfunction at the union, the financial plight, the disputes, the emptying stadiums, the defeats – oh, the defeats – feel a very long way away. The All Blacks have been beaten. Seventy-three years of hurt, no more need for dreaming.

The euphoria in the Principality Stadium, however many people were there – or more pertinently not – seemed as eerily familiar as it was cathartic. This was how Cardiff used to feel on match day.

Continue reading...
title: History, euphoria and no more dreaming – are Wales back after win over All Blacks? | Michael Aylwin

author: Rory Carroll
description:
Hundreds of thousands expected to rally against plan to scrap licence fees and fund broadcasters from state budget

Hundreds of thousands of Czechs are expected to rally in Prague on Sunday to protest against what they say is a government attempt to stifle media freedom.

The gathering to save the mandatory licence fees that fund Czechia’s public broadcasters could be one of the biggest in the nation’s history, organisers say.

Continue reading...
title: Protest in Prague over media freedom expected to be one of biggest in Czechia’s history

author: Huw Baines
description:
Bristol Beacon
The UK artist combines feminist fury with accessible melodies and a dramatic flair that sees her alternately pogoing and seeking out the wind machines at the prow of the stage

People are dancing to a song they don’t know, with flower garlands in their hair and their arms around their friends. This reaction to Fairy Dance, an unreleased track written about the community that has sprung up around her music, says a lot about the moment Paris Paloma finds herself in, and tonight’s show feels for all the world like a stepping stone to bigger things.

Throughout, Paloma leans in to the built-in drama of songs from her second album, The Fatal Flaw, which pairs ornate folk arrangements with the sort of arena-sized alt-pop production favoured by Florence + the Machine. With a sculpture inspired by surrealist Ithell Colquhoun
title: Paris Paloma review – arena-scale alt-pop drama from a singer on her way to bigger things

author: Aamna Mohdin
description:
Acorn, a community union, is helping people fight unfair bills, AI decision-making and housing injustices as cost-of-living crisis deepens

Yasmin didn’t expect to find herself sitting across a negotiating table from executives at one of Britain’s biggest water companies. But her growing frustration with her water bills had led her to launch a national campaign.

The 34-year-old single mother from Manchester had endured unexplained charges and a nine-month wait for a water meter. She went to the community union Acorn to propose a campaign that would in time force four major water companies into negotiations. United Utilities eventually apologised for its handling of her case and credited £250 to her account.

Continue reading...
title: ‘Nobody else is going to save us’: the direct action group taking on the UK’s banks, bailiffs and water firms

author: Jasper Jolly
description:
Liberty Steel Dalzell plant in Motherwell with order for 34,000 tonnes of metal plate to build three warships has struggled to pay bills

The Royal Navy is facing questions over whether three new warships will be built with British steel as its Scottish supplier faces deepening financial difficulties.

Liberty Steel Dalzell, a plate mill in Motherwell, has struggled to pay its bills and workers in recent weeks, according to several people with knowledge of operations.

Continue reading...
title: Troubled Scottish steel supplier raises questions over Royal Navy contracts

author: Lisa O’Carroll Senior correspondent
description:
Delayed deliveries and inspection hold-ups among issues facing hauliers navigating post-Brexit border processes

Three small boxes of spinach and ricotta cannelloni destined for a supermarket in Gibraltar languish on an EU inspector’s bench at the Eurotunnel terminal in Calais.

They have been removed from a truck laden with perishables for British food lovers on the Rock – Morrisons steak and ale pie, family-size blocks of Morrisons cheddar cheese, ‘M’ Best coleslaw from Avondale foods in Craigavon in Northern Ireland and long-life milk.

Continue reading...
title: Pasta, pies and paperwork errors: the reality of Brexit food checks

author: Oliver Milman in Antalya
description:
Strongest El Niño in centuries adds urgency to UN climate talks as vulnerable countries face ‘compounding’ crises

If the galloping pace of the climate crisis isn’t enough to spur countries to act at UN climate talks under way in Turkey, there is another major threat heightening its havoc: the strongest El Niño event in at least 1,000 years.

The “jaw-dropping” El Niño, a naturally recurring phenomenon where the eastern Pacific heats up every few years with temporary but global implications, has provided added urgency to wrangling at the Cop31 summit over climate funding for vulnerable countries that are having to scramble to respond.

Continue reading...
title: ‘Risk multiplier’: super El Niño looms over Cop31 as climate pattern fuels global disasters

author: Agencies
description:
Fears for national entrance exam next week, as top scorer on tax exam admits sending photos of questions to AI tool

The marks attained by the top scorer ⁠on South Korea’s national exam for aspiring tax accountants this year seemed too good to be true. On Sunday, sceptics were ⁠proven right when he ⁠confessed to ​using generative AI to cheat.

The scandal follows months of speculation after he scored near-perfect marks on hundreds of questions over two exams ⁠taken in April and July. It has also raised the stakes for organisers of South Korea’s annual college entrance exam this Thursday.

Continue reading...
title: AI cheating scandal rattles South Korea as annual college exam looms

author: Xaymaca Awoyungbo
description:
• All the latest news from around the footballing world

  • Get in touch: contact our matchday live writers on email

Hello and welcome to matchday live!

We have another big day of Nations League action after Norway overpowered Wales 3-1, Northern Ireland beat Ukraine 1-0 and Austria edged out Republic of Ireland 1-0 in yesterday’s fixtures.

Continue reading...
title: Spain v England Nations League buildup, WSL and more – matchday live

author: Billy Munday at Cherry Red Records Stadium
description:
Clubs with wealthy proprietors can maintain a loss-making operation but things can be more complex when the supporters carry the can

When you walk up from Haydons Road train station to Plough Lane there is a blue AFC Wimbledon billboard that reads “Fan owned football”, directly opposite the site of the old Plough Lane stadium where there are now blocks of flats. There is a memorial to the old Wimbledon FC – a reminder that supporters can often have little say in the running of their club – on the same corner, just up the road from the new Cherry Red Records Stadium.

AFC Wimbledon are one of only two majority fan-owned clubs in the EFL – along with Exeter City – but that makes running a loss-making operation, as 94% of teams in England’s top five tiers are doing according to the State of the Game report, even more challenging. “In other clubs, the owner just puts their hand in their pocket, produces cash,” said Hannah Kitcher, who has been a member of the Dons Trust Boar
title: AFC Wimbledon, a failed £87m investment bid and the challenge for fan ownership

author: As told to Nick Ames
description:
The former England centre-back answers your questions on Diego Maradona, Bobby Robson and on staying in strange places

“Have you made up all these on your own?” asks Terry Butcher, sitting in a London office in the week he is presented with his England legacy cap. It turns out dozens of Guardian readers want to pick the brains of a much-loved centre-back who was feted en route to a World Cup semi-final and tormented four years previously by the mercurial genius of Diego Maradona.

Did Maradona ever admit to the “Hand of God”? Butcher found himself in the post-match doping-control room alongside his nemesis at the Azteca in 1986. “I tapped my head, then my hand, and then he tapped his head,” Butcher says. “He didn’t admit to it because, if he had, I’d have been right across that room.”

Continue reading...
title: Terry Butcher: ‘I’ve learned to live with the Hand of God goal better’

author: Tumaini Carayol
description:
Winning his first two grand slams and leading the rankings should be cause for celebration, but the German benefited from a vacuum at the top

Alexander Zverev had plenty of thoughts in the miserable aftermath of his loss at the Paris Masters last week, a 7-6 (5), 6-2 second-round defeat by Lorenzo Musetti marking him as the first ATP No 1 to lose his first match as the top-ranked player in straight sets.

Rather than feeling any pressure surrounding his new status in the buildup to the final Masters 1000 tournament of the year, Zverev had simply been annoyed. “Achieving the world No 1 status is something every player dreams of, but I feel like I’m the only world No 1 in tennis history that has to explain why it’s OK for me to be world No 1. Which I find quite difficult, because I think I deserve to be where I am, even though I lost today.”

Continue reading...
title: Alexander Zverev’s troubled start as world No 1 sums up dismal year for men’s tennis | Tumaini Carayol

author: Ebony Riddell Bamber
description:
In the 90s, I studied under the notorious racist lecturer Frank Ellis. At a time when I should have felt liberated to explore, it chipped away at my self-esteem

In 2006, Dr Frank Ellis, who taught Russian and Slavonic studies at the University of Leeds, was suspended from his post as lecturer after he told a student newspaper that he supported the theory that Black people were less intelligent than white people. In the pages of the Guardian at the time, he was described as a “lecturer who insisted that black people and women were genetically inferior”. This was six years after his views first received national coverage.

When I saw Ellis’s views make it to the national press, I felt angry. I had known Ellis was a racist because when I was a student of Russian studies between 1996 and 2000, he taught many of my clas
title: Oxford is platforming race baiter Nathan Cofnas. I know how corrosive that will be for Black students | Ebony Riddell Bamber

author: Joe Pinner
description:
Dutch designer sets up an app to help fellow enthusiasts find the great trees of the world

While most people spend their holidays sightseeing or lazing by a pool, Hidde Burgmans would rather seek out special trees.

While not an expert in the subject, the 37-year-old from Baarn in the Netherlands has developed what he cheerfully admits is something of an obsession. He even managed to propose to his girlfriend, Nadia Roeleveld, under a particularly special cedar in Japan: “My fiancee always laughs, because she’s like, ‘OK, we have to make a detour again because Hidde found another big tree’.”

Continue reading...
title: Looking for an ancient tree worth a detour? There’s an app for that

author: Natricia Duncan Caribbean correspondent
description:
In their book, the historian Nicole Phillip and journalist Laura Trevelyan use connected experiences to show how reparations can work in practice

When the Grenadian historian Nicole Phillip opened an email from the then BBC journalist Laura Trevelyan in 2022, she uncovered a connection that stretched back centuries.

Their ancestors had stood on opposite sides of enslavement in Grenada: Phillip’s among Africans forcibly taken from their homes and enslaved, Trevelyan’s among the British families who profited from a system that inflicted unspeakable cruelty and inhumanity on generations of enslaved Africans.

Continue reading...
title: Entangled Past: how descendants of enslaved and enslavers in Grenada embarked on journey of repair

author: Jane Clinton and Nicola Slawson
description:
In the second in our series, four young Britons reveal how the search has taken a toll on their mental and physical health

  • ‘The social contract is broken’: young people on feeling shut out of careers

  • Guardian to follow lives of eight young people in their search for jobs

“I had to quit and move back in with my parents because I had developed ME/chronic fatigue syndrome. I am now housebound and cannot look after myself. Although I cannot prove it, I strongly believe that prolonged period of high stress played a big part in the decline of my health.”

Continue reading...
title: ‘I’m scared about my future’: young people on the stress and desperation of jobseeking

author: Severin Carrell Scotland editor
description:
Scientists succeed in breeding wild oysters in Dornoch Firth, near Inverness, from where they disappeared more than 100 years ago

The baby oysters, with their rough cream-coloured shells and ragged edges, are about the size of a 50 pence piece. But off the north-east coast of Scotland, they are proof of a breakthrough in marine conservation.

For the first time in the UK, scientists have succeeded in breeding wild oysters at a site where they had been locally extinct for more than a century, in the Dornoch Firth north of Inverness.

Continue reading...
title: Return of the wild oyster: conservationists bring shellfish back from local extinction off Scottish coast

author: Emma Gibbs
description:
As a lone female traveller, the prospect of staying in a hut on Rannoch Moor is daunting, but the silence of the mountains and lochs turns out to be ‘the ultimate luxury’

In the gloaming, the trees stand dark and impenetrable on either side of the path. An owl, wide-faced and pale as a spectre, glides out of the pines ahead of me. Heart pounding, I pick up speed and continue uphill, the silence thick around me.

Just a few minutes earlier, I had been scuffing my feet in the sand by the loch shore, watching as the clouds draped themselves across the top of the Grampians. In the absence of other people, Loch Laidon, silvery in the half-light, had been mine to enjoy; in the woods, however, my solitude feels unnerving.

Continue reading...
title: ‘I was nervous before my solo stay in a remote Scottish Highlands cabin – but the solitude is glorious’

author: Shane Hickey
description:
Unlike familiar Captcha tests, this con asks you to press a series of keys. And that’s a way in for fraudsters to install malicious software

You are looking for some gifts for Christmas and want to support small businesses when you shop. When you visit the site of one you’ve heard good things about you are asked to verify that you are human.

Instead of clicking on a series of images, or typing letters that appear, just as you have seen before, you are asked to press a series of keys and then press enter.

Continue reading...
title: ‘Prove you are not a robot’: how the Captcha scam captures your computer

author: Phil Harrison, Priya Elan, Jack Seale, Graeme Virtue and Simon Wardell
description:
Undercover cameras paint a bleak portrait of the situation. Plus, it’s sea lion v black neck swan in Blue Planet III. Here’s what to watch this evening

10pm, ITV1

Continue reading...
title: TV tonight: a tough look inside Crowborough asylum camp

author: Steve Bloomfield
description:
Lana Nusseibeh appears to have the support of Russia and the US, but her role glossing the horror in Sudan makes her unsuitable – and we should say so

Since the devastating war in Sudan began in 2023, some of the best investigative work uncovering those responsible has been carried out by the UN panel of experts. Its reports have revealed clear evidence that the United Arab Emirates (UAE) has been funnelling weapons and providing mercenaries to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a Sudanese paramilitary group that has been accused of genocide.

It is these reports, produced by UN-funded investigato
title: Britain’s veto could stop the UAE’s choice from running the United Nations. Miliband must use it | Steve Bloomfield

author: Mark Sweney
description:
Exclusive: British sportswear firm is seeking to obtain rights to The Conditioning Club, which is also the name of a Gloucestershire gym

Gymshark, the £1bn British sportswear firm started in a family garage, is locked in a trademark battle that threatens the future of a small fitness business.

Ben Francis, the university dropout who started sewing his own gym clothes in his parents’ garage and is now estimated to be worth £800m, is trying to add The Conditioning Club to his Gymshark stable of trademarks.

Continue reading...
title: Gymshark in trademark battle that threatens future of small fitness business

author: Meera Sodha
description:
After a childhood of grief, hardship and hunger, the Guardian food writer’s father Raj always resisted going back to Uganda. What happened when he finally agreed to accompany her on a bittersweet journey into the past?

The moment I step off the plane and on to the soil of Entebbe it hits me. Uganda is in my blood. This country that had once existed only in my imagination is finally real. The heat is heavy, the earth bright and rich like dark terracotta. I want to capture this moment – me with my 75-year-old dad, back where he was born. A place he never imagined he would return to. I whoop and reach for my camera, turn it towards my father’s face.

“You’re back!” I say.

Continue reading...
title: ‘Like many men of his generation, he tends to push his feelings down from his heart to his toes’: Meera Sodha on her father’s homecoming

author: Grace Dent
description:
Ever-open, eminently relatable, sensibly priced spots of this sort will always have an audience

A London chophouse has taken up residence on St Philip’s Place, Birmingham, on the edge of Cathedral Square, or “Pigeon Park”, as the locals call it. This particular nook of Brum city centre is a magnet to those feathered blighters, although Blacklock’s smoulderingly macho menu is ironically pigeon-meat free, revolving instead around heaps of chops and steaks cooked over charcoal. There’s porterhouse, bone-in sirloin, lamb rump and pig’s head on toast.

Launched in London in 2015, Blacklock was the elegant, edgy, no-nonsense dining experience for groovy young things who quite literally wanted meat and two veg, so long as said veg was dripping-fat chips; it now has five sites in the capital and another in Manche
title: Blacklock, Birmingham B3: ‘A very, very cool version of an Angus Steakhouse’ – restaurant review

author: Nick Robins-Early
description:
Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected spy is Silicon Valley’s worst nightmare come true

The resignation this week of Nvidia’s founder and CEO Jensen Huang is one of the most astonishing corporate scandals in memory, featuring allegations of international espionage and extramarital affairs involving one of the world’s most powerful men. As investigations mount into what went wrong at the $4tn chip company, the saga may also become a milestone in the decades-long history of spies infiltrating the US tech industry.

Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife of 41 years in a letter to employees this past weekend, following a report from the New York Times that the tech mogul had a close relationship with a woman US officials suspect of spying for China’s government. Huang resigned
title: ‘Jensen Huang lost his mind’: how AI’s smartest man fell for the world’s oldest trick

author: Camille Corcoran and Rajeev Syal
description:
Thames Water says detainees at proposed accommodation should expect to experience insect swarms and strong smells

A Home Office plan to build asylum seeker detention facilities next to a sewage pump is facing objections after water company officials warned that detainees should expect to experience insect swarms and strong smells.

Proposed secure accommodation blocks at Campsfield House immigration removal centre in Oxfordshire will be 20 metres from a sewage pumping station, according to a written submission from Thames Water.

Continue reading...
title: Planned asylum seeker detention centre next to Oxfordshire sewage works criticised

author: Oliver Holmes and Kaamil Ahmed
description:
International court of justice has never before found a state guilty of genocide, and ruling will have implications for case against Israel

The world’s top court will deliver a judgment this week on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, in a landmark case that will set a critical 21st-century benchmark for the gravest of all international crimes.

The closely watched judgment could become one of the most significant moments in international law since the end of the second world war.

Continue reading...
title: World’s top court to rule if Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya

author: Megan Maurice
description:
• Updates as the Jillaroos and Kiwi Ferns meet in the decider in Brisbane

  • Kick-off time is 3.10pm local/4.10pm AEDT/5.10am BST

  • Any thoughts? Send us an email

The teams have entered the field now for the pre-match ceremony – not long to go until kick off.

The weather is muggy and humid in Brisbane today – it’s currently 28.6 degrees and 72% humidity. Both teams will have to be smart in how they manage their benches to reduce the impact of fatigue.

Continue reading...
title: Australia v New Zealand: Women’s Rugby League World Cup final – live

author: Polly Hudson
description:
As teenagers, my friends and I thought it was glamorous to have relationships with older men. But after the revelations about Russell Brand and David Walliams, I have started to see that period of my life in a new light

It has been a strange time to be a “woman of a certain age”, as Gregg Wallace so charmingly labelled us. Many of us were consumed by every detail of the Russell Brand trial and the David Walliams exposé. We were pleasantly surprised, albeit dazed – stunned even – by there being consequences for their behaviour, because that’s not how it usually goes, in our experience.

A few d
title: At 17, I dated a 36-year-old. That decision looks very different to me now | Polly Hudson

author: Angelique Chrisafis in Vincennes and Paris
description:
Educators voice concerns as thousands of children facing exams miss up to 150 hours of class

For several weeks, Alex, 16, has woken at 4am and walked 90 minutes in the dark from his northern Paris suburb so he can help gather wheelie bins to blockade his high school in Vincennes.

In a tote bag, he brings some masks and some swimming goggles in case of police teargas. His parents, who work in the arts and vote left, support the French school student protesters who since September have blocked schools demanding repairs to dilapidated school buildings, more replacement teachers, a solution to overcrowded classes and more equality in the uni
title: ‘We need to get back to class’: some teachers lose patience as France enters its eighth week of student protests

author: Guardian staff and agencies
description:
Order by judge Ana Reyes is the latest instance of the federal judiciary pushing back against Trump’s efforts to redesign the nation’s capital

A federal judge has ordered a temporary suspension of any work at a historic Washington public golf course, in the latest setback for US president Donald Trump’s plan to turn it ⁠into a championship-level course.

In a 30-page decision, US district judge Ana Reyes temporarily blocked the federal government from moving forward with a plan that would have closed East Potomac Park on Sunday. Trump said in an 18 ⁠October social media post that the closure would last 15 months and transform the park’s golf offerings into “one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World”.

Continue reading...
title: US judge blocks Trump’s plan to renovate historic DC golf course

author: Oliver Holmes and Rebecca Bailey
description:
Tussle for influence as trade, tech and regional security to take centre stage in China, Philippines and Cambodia meetings

The global political centre of gravity will be firmly in Asia this week as world leaders fly in for back-to-back high-level summits against the backdrop of the tussle for influence between the superpowers China and the US.

Beijing will have the home advantage when it welcomes Donald Trump to its southern technology hub of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders’ meeting. It starts two weeks after the US leader lost midterm elections.

Continue reading...
title: World leaders head to Asia for back-to-back diplomatic summits

author: Guardian staff and agencies
description:
Ukrainian president says Kyiv not ready to concede Donbas but would put idea to a referendum in exchange for security guarantees and funding. What we know on day 1,726

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the US has asked for the first time if Ukraine would withdraw from parts of the eastern Donbas region that Russia does not control in exchange for Ukraine becoming a Nato member. But the Ukrainian president said his country would not surrender territory. “The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?’,” he said in remarks to reporters released by his office on Saturday. “That is why ⁠I believe Nato is back on the agenda.” But he said the suggestion, which would form part of a new postwar security framework for Europe, could allow Russia to weaken Nato and reshape borders. “This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations,” Zelenskyy said.

<
title: Ukraine war briefing: US proposes Kyiv cede land to Russia for Nato membership, Zelenskyy says

author: Guardian Staff
description:
The best photographs from the first Eurovision Asia, held in Bangkok, Thailand. Artists from 11 countries competed in the inaugural Asian edition of the contest, staged 70 years after the original Eurovision song contest made its debut

  • Philippines’ Carmelle wins first Eurovision contest in Asia

Continue reading...
title: The inaugural Eurovision Asia 2026 – in pictures

author: Raphael Boyd and Press Association
description:
Deputy prime minister says change would be a massive step but ‘deserves proper consideration and scrutiny’

The government has said it will consider calls to change the age of consent after a woman waived her right to anonymity to publicly claim she was raped by Russell Brand as a 16-year-old schoolgirl.

Mia Latter, now 37, alleged she had been orally raped by the jailed comedian when she was a teenager and he was 30 years old.

Continue reading...
title: UK government to consider changing age of consent after allegations against Russell Brand
